definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) can be used to automate aspects of the job recruitment process.
details: Advances in AI, such as the advent of machine learning and the growth of big data, enable AI to be utilized to recruit, screen, and predict the success of applicants. Proponents of AI in hiring claim it reduces bias, assists with finding qualified candidates, and frees up human resource (HR) workers' time for other tasks, while opponents worry that AI perpetuates inequalities in the workplace and will eliminate jobs. Despite potential benefits, the ethical implications of AI in hiring remain a subject of debate, with concerns about algorithmic transparency, accountability, and the need for ongoing oversight to ensure fair and unbiased decision-making throughout the recruitment process.

explainer.lead: Artificial intelligence in hiring means using AI to automate parts of recruitment, such as screening applicants or predicting their likely success. It could help employers find qualified candidates and save HR workers time, but it also raises serious questions about bias, transparency, accountability, and oversight.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a helper that sorts a huge pile of job applications and points out people who seem suited to the job. That can save time, but the helper may make unfair choices if it has learned unfair patterns. People therefore still need to check how it works and whether it treats everyone fairly.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply machine learning to large collections of applicant data to support recruitment, screening, and candidate-success prediction within HR workflows. The main pitfalls are reproducing workplace inequalities, making decisions that are hard to explain, and deploying models without continuing human oversight. Monitoring for fair and unbiased decision-making remains necessary throughout recruitment.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, an applicant can be represented by features x, with a machine-learning model f(x) used to support screening or estimate predicted success. Supporters propose gains in candidate discovery, reduced bias, and HR efficiency, but these benefits are contested. Known concerns include perpetuated inequality, job displacement, limited algorithmic transparency, unclear accountability, and the need for ongoing oversight.

explainer.example: An employer receiving more applications than its HR team can comfortably review uses AI to screen them and highlight apparently qualified candidates. The system may also estimate applicants' likely success, while HR staff continue the recruitment work and monitor whether the automated decisions are fair.

usedIn.name: Human resources

explainer.intuition: The basic idea is to let software handle some of the repetitive work of sorting and assessing applicants. Its usefulness depends not only on accurate predictions, but also on whether its decisions are fair, understandable, and properly supervised.
howItWorks: Applicant information is collected for use in the recruitment process.
Machine-learning methods draw on that data to support recruitment or screening.
The system may identify qualified candidates or predict applicants' likely success.
HR workers use the resulting assistance while retaining other recruitment responsibilities.
Ongoing oversight checks transparency, accountability, and fairness in decision-making.
explainer.whyItMatters: Hiring affects people's access to work, so automation can have consequences well beyond administrative efficiency. AI might save time and help surface qualified candidates, but unfair or opaque decisions could reinforce workplace inequalities.
misconceptions: AI in hiring is automatically less biased than human decision-making; opponents warn that it can perpetuate inequality.
Using AI means recruiters are no longer needed; HR workers still have other tasks, and ongoing oversight remains important.
Good predictions alone make a hiring system acceptable; transparency, accountability, and fairness also matter.
